description:
FARAD SPACE is the space branch of FARAD Robotics, one of Azerbaijan's first student robotics and engineering teams, founded in Baku in 2020. Our members study mechatronics, robotics, software and data science, and we build space and aviation systems, CubeSats, rockets, drones, underwater robots (AUVs) and AI tools.

For NASA Space Apps 2026 (Planet X and SPHEREx) we built SkyLapse, a free public web tool that joins 16 years of NASA WISE/NEOWISE and SPHEREx infrared images into one movie, so anyone can watch nearby stars and brown dwarfs move and see their SPHEREx spectra. Live tool: skylapse.vercel.app
summary: SkyLapse is a free, public web tool that turns 16 years of NASA infrared images into one movie of the sky, so anyone can see what moves. SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours, but its own record is only about a year long, so even nearby cold objects shift by just a pixel or two. SkyLapse joins SPHEREx (2025–2026) with NASA WISE/NEOWISE (2010–2024) at the same 4.6-micron wavelength, places every image on one common sky grid and plays them as a single blink movie. Type a star name or coordinates, press play, and brown dwarfs and fast stars crawl across the screen. Click an object to see its SPHEREx spectrum, its light curve and a plain-language explanation in English or Azerbaijani, written only from our own measurements. You can also drive the viewer by voice. We validated SkyLapse on all five NASA test targets: measured motions agree with ESA Gaia and the literature to better than 99%, R Draconis' 246-day period matches AAVSO, and a blind search recovered 3 of 3 known movers with no false alarms.
details:
What it does

SkyLapse is a "time machine" for the infrared sky, built for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Enter a star name or coordinates and it plays every NASA infrared image of that patch from 2010 to 2026 as one blink movie.

  • 16-year movie: WISE/NEOWISE epochs (2010–2024) plus SPHEREx epochs (2025–2026), reprojected onto one common sky grid (2.75″ per pixel). Sequences: 4.6 µm (WISE W2 + SPHEREx detector D6), 3.4 µm (WISE W1 + SPHEREx D4) and SPHEREx-only (D1–D6). Play, step, speed, contrast, zoom and full screen; the timeline shows which telescope took each frame.
  • Compare times: difference images and co-adds over a chosen time range make moving objects pop out.
  • Overlays: ESA Gaia DR3 stars moved to each frame's date, CatWISE2020 sources, the target's measured track, and masks for saturated or flagged pixels (overlay accuracy 0.04–0.12 px, about 0.3″).
  • Spectral fingerprint: the SPHEREx spectrum of a clicked source (forced photometry at its moving position) and an RGB composite of detectors D1/D3/D6.
  • Light curves for variable stars.
  • Blind search: detects sources in every epoch, links them across 16 years, fits a proper motion and labels each object "known mover", "candidate" or "artifact". We never call anything a discovery; candidates are for scientists to follow up.
  • Any sky position: a live service builds a new WISE field on request in about 15–33 seconds and marks the fastest Gaia movers.
  • Ask SkyLapse: voice or text commands ("show WISE 0855", "play faster", "show the spectrum") are turned into a fixed list of safe viewer actions.
  • Plain-language explanations in English and Azerbaijani, generated only from our computed numbers.
  • Shareable: the full view state lives in the URL.

Why it matters

SPHEREx alone covers only about one year, so even the fastest nearby objects move by just a pixel or two between its images. Adding 14 years of WISE/NEOWISE at the same wavelength stretches the baseline to 16 years, so the same objects move by 70–170 arcseconds and are obvious to the eye. To our knowledge no open interactive tool joins the 16-year WISE motion record with SPHEREx spectra in one view.

Validation on all five NASA test targets

  • Barnard's Star: 10,395 ± 17 mas/yr vs 10,393 mas/yr (Gaia DR3), 99.8% agreement.
  • WISE 0855−0714: 8,157 ± 15 mas/yr vs 8,152 mas/yr (Kirkpatrick et al. 2021), 99.9%. Its SPHEREx spectrum shows no flux below 2.4 µm or in the 3.3 µm methane band and a detection at 4.4–4.9 µm, as expected for a ~250 K Y dwarf.
  • ε Indi B: 4,717 ± 10 vs 4,684 mas/yr, 99.0%; it moves together with ε Indi A (99.3% agreement), confirming a bound system.
  • R Draconis: period 246 days vs 246.12 days (AAVSO VSX), measured from the unsaturated outer wings of the star.
  • RW Aurigae: our brightness index tracks NEOWISE photometry (r = 0.93–0.98).
  • Blind search: recovered 3 of 3 NASA movers with 0 false candidates in 5 fields.

Motions are fitted over up to 46 WISE epochs spanning 14 years. We flag honestly where data fail: Barnard's Star and R Draconis saturate SPHEREx in nearly every image.

How it works

A Python pipeline (Astropy, astroquery, reproject, photutils, NumPy, SciPy) queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx images by position (no hard-coded file lists, so new data releases are picked up automatically), uses the flag, variance and zodiacal-light layers, co-adds per detector and epoch, fetches time-resolved unWISE coadds of WISE/NEOWISE, reprojects everything onto one grid and exports a small static bundle. A React + TypeScript web app (Vite, Canvas 2D) renders the frames in the browser. A FastAPI service resolves names, builds new fields and runs Ask SkyLapse. The five NASA targets are precomputed, so the demo never depends on a live archive.

Benefits and intended impact

SkyLapse makes the newest NASA mission data understandable in a minute, in a browser, for free. It gives students and citizen scientists the blink method that let NASA's Backyard Worlds volunteers find cold brown dwarfs, now with SPHEREx colours and a 16-year baseline, and it gives astronomers a quick vetting view for candidate movers. First users: university students and school programs in Azerbaijan, with a bilingual English/Azerbaijani interface.

How it is creative

Instead of a plain SPHEREx image browser, SkyLapse treats two NASA missions as one 16-year experiment: WISE supplies the motion, SPHEREx supplies the colour. Saturated stars are measured from their unsaturated wings, and voice commands let people use the tool without learning astronomy software.

What we considered

Scientific honesty (measured numbers only, no "discovery" claims, saturation flagged), a demo that works offline from precomputed data, low cost (free hosting), and being polite to public archives (caching, limited parallel requests).

What's next

Weekly updates as SPHEREx releases new data, automatic candidate lists, more languages, a "flag this mover" button for volunteers and a classroom program with universities.

Tools and languages

Python 3.11, Astropy, astroquery, reproject, photutils, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI, TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Canvas 2D, Web Speech API, Vercel, Railway, GitHub.

Links

Live tool: https://skylapse.vercel.app
Source code: https://github.com/FARADTechnologies/NASA2026
Methodology: https://github.com/FARADTechnologies/NASA2026/blob/main/docs/METHODOLOGY.md

Use of AI (SI)

Our team came up with the idea, designed the product, chose the data and methods, checked the science and validated every result against Gaia and the literature. We used AI tools as assistants: Claude Code (Anthropic) helped us write and debug the code and documentation faster, and every change was reviewed and tested by the team. AI also helped with text editing, English/Azerbaijani translation and some illustrations in our local pitch slides. Inside the product, two features use AI on purpose: the short object explanations are generated by Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 only from numbers our pipeline measured (every number is checked automatically and the site labels the text as AI-generated), and Ask SkyLapse uses a Claude model to turn a spoken or typed request into one of a fixed list of viewer actions, with an offline fallback. All scientific data comes from NASA and ESA, not from AI. The demo video is a screen recording of the live site; its English voiceover is AI-generated (ElevenLabs). No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers were generated or modified by AI.
